title: Vice-Chair Decision Patterns: Ethical Analysis Framework
status: ANALYSIS PENDING - Script created, execution requires ethical review
purpose: Detect SYSTEMIC inconsistency in WSIAT decision-making, NOT individual bias targeting

ethicalConsiderations.primaryConcern: Publishing individual vice-chair success rates could enable 'judge shopping' and unfairly bias perceptions
potentialHarms: Appellants may delay hearings to get 'favorable' vice-chair
Vice-chairs may face public criticism for decisions in complex cases
Media may sensationalize outliers without understanding case mix
System gaming could undermine legitimacy of WSIAT
Unfair to vice-chairs who hear more complex/difficult cases
potentialBenefits: Detection of systemic bias (e.g., against certain injury types)
ethicalConsiderations.balancingTest: Publish IF systemic inconsistency detected AND cannot be explained by case mix AND serves public interest
redLines: ❌ NEVER suggest appellants request specific vice-chairs
❌ NEVER publish without expert legal review
❌ NEVER attribute outliers to 'bias' without controlling for case complexity

step2_consistencyAnalysis.limitation: Only 6.1% of decisions have detectable outcomes (keyword matching)
controls: Injury type distribution (some injuries harder to prove)
Representation quality (union vs self-rep vs clinic)
Panel composition (full panel vs vice-chair only)

step3_caseMixAdjustment.problem: Vice-chairs hearing more chronic pain cases will have lower success rates (harder to prove)
step3_caseMixAdjustment.solution: Compare success rates WITHIN injury types
step3_caseMixAdjustment.example: Vice-Chair A: 10% success on back injuries. Vice-Chair B: 40% success on back injuries. Same injury, different outcomes.
step3_caseMixAdjustment.method: Stratified analysis by injury type, industry, panel composition
step3_caseMixAdjustment.limitation: Requires large sample sizes per stratum (may not have enough data)

step4_outlierInvestigation.definition: Vice-chair >2 standard deviations from mean success rate
possibleExplanations: Hears more complex cases (referred from other panels)
step4_outlierInvestigation.ethicalResponse: Report outlier EXISTS, explain possible causes, do NOT attribute to bias without evidence

publishIF: Cannot be explained by case mix
step5_publicationDecision.anonymizationOption: Report patterns without naming vice-chairs (e.g., 'Vice-Chair Group A' vs 'Vice-Chair Group B')

scenario1_lowVariance.publicationDecision: Do NOT publish - no systemic concern

scenario2_moderateVariance.publicationDecision: Investigate outliers, publish if not explained by case mix
scenario2_moderateVariance.message: Some variation detected, requires deeper analysis

scenario3_highVariance.publicationDecision: Publish with ethical disclosure, advocate for standardization

IF_publishingRequired.title: WSIAT Decision Consistency Analysis
structure: Executive Summary (systemic finding, not individual blame)
Aggregate Statistics (mean, variance, range - NO NAMES)
Case Mix Analysis (injury type, industry, representation)
Disclosure (cannot determine individual bias, case mix matters)
IF_publishingRequired.anonymization: Report 'Quintile 1' vs 'Quintile 5' success rates, NOT individual names
IF_publishingRequired.focusOnSystem: Emphasize systemic issues (need for training, clearer standards), NOT individual vice-chairs

approach1_aggregateOnly.method: Report overall consistency statistics without individual data
approach1_aggregateOnly.pros: Avoids judge shopping, focuses on system
approach1_aggregateOnly.cons: Less transparent, cannot detect individual outliers

approach2_confidentialReport.method: Share findings with WSIAT Chair, legal clinics ONLY (not public)

approach3_injuryTypeOnly.method: Report consistency within injury types (e.g., 'back injury appeals vary 5%-35%')
approach3_injuryTypeOnly.pros: Focuses on systemic issues, not individuals
approach3_injuryTypeOnly.cons: Still detectable who specific vice-chairs are

approach4_noPublication.method: Collect data, do NOT publish, use for internal advocacy only

implementation: Report: 'Back injury appeals success rate varies 8%-22% depending on panel'
Report: 'Chronic pain appeals success rate varies 3%-18%'
Report: 'Mental health appeals success rate varies 5%-25%'
Focus on NEED for standardization, training, clearer evidence standards
recommendedApproach.message: WSIAT outcomes too dependent on which panel you get - system needs reform

requiredBeforePublication.question: Will this data help or harm injured workers?
How will you respond to this analysis?
requiredBeforePublication.concern: Opportunity to explain case mix, training efforts

requiredBeforePublication.question: Does this serve systemic reform goals?

legalConsiderations.publicRecord: WSIAT decisions are public record, vice-chair names already published
legalConsiderations.defamation: Risk if publication suggests individual bias without evidence
legalConsiderations.mitigation: Focus on systemic patterns, careful language, expert review

comparisonToOtherJurisdictions.usCourtAnalytics: Many U.S. states publish judicial decision statistics (case outcomes, sentencing patterns)
comparisonToOtherJurisdictions.ukTransparency: UK publishes tribunal success rates by jurisdiction
comparisonToOtherJurisdictions.canadaPrecedent: Limited - some law schools analyze judicial patterns for research
comparisonToOtherJurisdictions.lesson: Transparency increasing, but MUST be done carefully with ethical safeguards

nextSteps.step7: IF consensus to publish, use anonymized injury-type approach

conclusionForThisProject.decision: Script created, analysis PENDING stakeholder consultation
conclusionForThisProject.rationale: Ethical concerns outweigh immediate benefit without expert review
conclusionForThisProject.transparency: This framework itself demonstrates commitment to ethical research
conclusionForThisProject.message: We CAN analyze vice-chair patterns, but MUST do it responsibly
